sources.title: HMRC: Claim Audio-Visual Expenditure Credits for Corporation Tax (last updated 19 February 2026)
sources.said: you can claim Audio-Visual Expenditure Credit ( AVEC ) on expenditure incurred from 1 January 2024 on: film high-end TV programmes children’s TV programmes animation … the programme is a drama, comedy, documentary, animation or children’s programme … a children’s programme if the primary audience for the programme is expected to be under the age of 15 … have average ‘core costs’ of at least £1 million for each hour of slot length have a slot length in relation to the programme which is greater than 20 minutes for each episode TV programmes commissioned together are treated as one programme. … Qualifying costs will be the lower of either: 80% of total core costs the amount of UK core costs … 39% of qualifying expenditure for children’s TV programmes, animated films and animated TV programmes … 34% on all other films and TV programmes … From 1 April 2025 films and TV programmes with a rate of 34% can claim further credit for visual effects costs. Costs incurred from 1 January 2025 are eligible. Visual effects costs have a rate of 39% and are exempt from the 80% cap on total core costs. Your company’s total expenditure credits for a period are taxed at the main rate of Corporation Tax.

sources.title: Screen Scotland: Broadcast Content Fund guidance (updated January 2024), linked from screen.scot/funding-and-support/funding/broadcast-content-fund
sources.said: The Fund has an allocation of £3m annually … Funding is awarded in the form of a recoupable grant. … Projects can be a series or a single programme. We will consider all genres but would particularly encourage applications from high-end television drama, live-action and animated children’s drama projects, and scripted comedy. We will only fund a proportion of the production costs of projects, and you must have secured, or have a written indication of, third party co-funding before making an application. … You must have secured, or have a written indication of, a broadcast commission, and/or a source of third party co-funding (excluding the UK creative industries tax reliefs) … we cannot fully fund the production costs of any project, regardless of the budget. … We do not have a minimum budget level for the projects we fund. … Awards for Production Funding are likely to be made in the range of £100,000–£500,000. … we would normally expect that at least 50% of the budget of any project is spent in Scotland. … Creative Scotland Broadcast Production Funding is an equity investment in the project and is recoupable and would be recouped alongside other equity funding prior to the project getting into net profits.

sources.title: Creative Wales Production Funding: Application Guidance (May 2023), linked from creative.wales/funding-and-support/production-funding

sources.title: SOLT & UK Theatre: Theatre in the UK 2026 (published 11 March 2026), pp. 16-17
sources.said: The West End generated record revenue of £1.084 billion in 2025 (up 4.1%) with 17.64 million attendances (up 3.16%). However, the number of performances grew slightly faster, rising by 3.26%. … average occupancy eased slightly to 84%. … The majority of tickets were sold at £56 or below, with more than a quarter under £35. … A West End play typically requires £1–2 million in upfront capital, with fixed weekly running costs of £120,000–£200,000 before royalties. … A West End musical may cost £3–10 million or more, with fixed weekly costs of £300,000–£400,000 … a production typically receives 70–81% of face value, and close to 60% where tickets are sold through third-party agents. A large musical may therefore need to gross £500,000 or more per week simply to break even. Even successful plays often recoup only late in their run, if at all.

figures.finding: A UK series claims the Audio-Visual Expenditure Credit on expenditure from 1 January 2024: 39% of qualifying expenditure for an animation or a children's programme (one whose audience is expected to be mostly under 15), 34% for the rest, which qualify only where average core expenditure reaches £1 million an hour of slot length and each episode's slot is over 20 minutes; qualifying expenditure is the lower of UK core expenditure and 80% of core expenditure.

No public fund across the UK backs a producer's live-action drama series: the BFI's UK Global Screen Fund takes television only as an international co-production in animation or documentary with two or three broadcasters in the finance; Screen Scotland's Broadcast Content Fund and Creative Wales's production funding each back work spent in their own nation (at least half the budget in Scotland; Welsh spend ten times the award). A production in the game names no nation, so none is read.

The BBC's tariff folds the independent producer's production fee into the price "in line with the Terms of Trade" and publishes no level; Screen Scotland asks only that overheads be reasonable, Creative Wales that a fee be proportionate. No cap is published.

Theatre Tax Relief, for accounting periods from 1 April 2025: a theatre tax credit of 45% of the loss surrendered for a touring production (six or more premises, or two or more and at least 14 performances, intended at the start of the production phase) and 40% otherwise; the additional deduction is the lower of UK qualifying expenditure and 80% of qualifying expenditure; the credits payable to an undertaking are at most 50 million euros a year.

Arts Council England's National Lottery Project Grants range from £1,000 to £100,000; in 2024/25, 9,332 eligible applications were received, with a success rate of 29.4% (36.6% in 2023/24), across every art form.

The UK's stage directors' minimum fees for a production: UK Theatre/Equity's freelance director in subsidised repertory, by the theatre's MRSL grade (from 6 April 2026: grade 1 £4,644.34, grade 2 £4,056.88, grade 3 £3,824.54; and each year from 3 July 2023), any week over four at 20% of the fee; SOLT/Equity's West End director by the theatre's category (from 6 April 2026: A, 1,100 seats and over, £7,347; B, 800 to 1,099, £6,390; C, up to 799, £5,809; and each year from 3 July 2023). The commercial rates (repertory, and tours and seasons by short or long run, normal or exceptional) were read, but the published card doesn't define the runs or the levels.

A playwright's minimums in the UK: UK Theatre/WGGB/SSP for subsidised theatres from 4 May 2026, by the theatre's MRSL grade, £11,598.60, £9,383.49 and £8,281.65 in all (on signature, delivery and acceptance), part an advance against a royalty of at least 8% of net box office; the ITC/WGGB for an ITC member's play, by its running time (over 70 minutes, 31 to 70, 11 to 30, 10 or less): 2025/26 (from 1 June 2025) £10,323.00, £6,873.75, £3,438.00, £1,000; 2026/27 £10,942.38, £7,286.18, £3,644.28, £1,060; 2027/28 £11,380.08, £7,577.62, £3,790.05, £1,102.40; royalty 8% from £61,807 net income. No West End (SOLT/WGGB) writers' agreement is published.

How a UK series reaches the screen: commissioned by a broadcaster at a licence fee (the BBC's tariff per hour, e.g. high-cost drama £650k to £1.1m), the producer deficit-financing the rest; 76 domestic UK high-end programmes started in 2025. No source counts how often a series financed without a broadcaster is picked up.

The West End took £1.084 billion from 17.64 million attendances in 2025; a West End play typically needs £1 to 2 million up front and £120,000 to £200,000 a week to run; "Even successful plays often recoup only late in their run, if at all." No UK source counts how often a production recoups; Bucknell's count (21% to 25.6% of Broadway musicals, 2008 to 2017) is another country's, a lead only.
